justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while the sidewalk on the right is comparatively narrow, indicating an imbalanced distribution of space among road users.
A raised curb and a continuous sidewalk are present on the right side, which provides some basic pedestrian access, but no curb ramps or tactile paving are visible in this view.
The grassy median and verge improve overall environmental quality, yet these planted areas do not directly function as usable space for pedestrians or cyclists.
No dedicated bicycle lane or shared-use path marking is visible, suggesting that cycling users receive less spatial provision than drivers.
safety: The carriageway is wide, smoothly paved, and clearly marked with lane lines, which supports orderly vehicle movement and reduces immediate collision risk for drivers.
A landscaped central median separates opposing traffic streams, which improves safety by lowering the chance of head-on conflicts.
Streetlights are installed along the corridor, supporting nighttime visibility and perceived safety.
However, the road geometry is broad and open, which may encourage higher driving speeds and increase risk severity for any crossing pedestrian or cyclist.
livability: The corridor appears clean, well maintained, and visually organized, which supports a baseline level of urban environmental quality.
Large blank walls on the right and campus- or industrial-style superblocks on the left create limited active frontage, reducing street life and social interaction.
There are no visible benches, kiosks, bus stops, or people engaged in street activity, so the street offers few cues of daily social convenience.
The setting feels more like a through-road than a mixed-use neighborhood street, which lowers everyday livability for non-drivers.
sustainability: The presence of grass medians and continuous rows of trees contributes to urban greenery and some ecological value.
The corridor is visually dominated by asphalt and private-vehicle space, which weakens support for low-carbon mode shift.
No dedicated cycling facility is visible, limiting sustainable transport options beyond driving.
Street trees along both sides can provide shade, carbon uptake, and some air-quality benefits, though their direct pedestrian benefit is uneven in this view.
aesthetics: The avenue has a coherent visual structure, with aligned streetlights, consistent lane markings, and a neat central green median.
Rows of trees on both sides soften the large roadway and improve the landscape character.
The street surface and curbs appear clean and well maintained, contributing to a polished visual impression.
At the same time, the long wall on the right and the very wide roadway create a somewhat monotonous, institutional appearance.
comfort: The asphalt surface is smooth and the roadway appears free of potholes, which improves physical comfort for drivers and potentially cyclists if they used the edge space.
Trees are present along both sides, but the pedestrian path visible on the right has limited direct shade at this moment, reducing thermal comfort.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or rest points, which lowers physical comfort for pedestrians spending time along the corridor.
Low visible congestion and a spacious cross-section may reduce stress for drivers, but the broad fast-road character can reduce psychological comfort for pedestrians and cyclists.
walkability: A sidewalk is visible on the right side and appears continuous, which provides a basic walking route.
The roadway is very wide and no marked crosswalk is visible in the scene, making pedestrian crossing likely difficult and reducing network permeability.
The right-side edge is lined by a long wall rather than active storefronts or entrances, so the walking experience lacks engagement and surveillance.
Although trees exist along the corridor, the pedestrian realm remains secondary to traffic space, limiting overall walk appeal.
bikeability: No painted bike lane, protected cycle track, or bicycle symbols are visible anywhere on the roadway or curbside.
The multi-lane avenue likely supports relatively high vehicle speeds, which makes mixed-traffic cycling feel unsafe for most users.
Raised curbs and narrow verge areas leave little clear evidence of a comfortable separated cycling route.
No bicycle parking, bike signals, or cycling wayfinding signs are visible, indicating weak support infrastructure for biking.
